credit-card-rewards.summary: Credit card reward value depends on eligible spending, earn rates, caps, redemption assumptions and fees. This worksheet separates recurring annual net value from a first-year bonus and compares two manual plans using the same spending budget.
credit-card-rewards.scope: Manual eligible-spending assumptions only. No issuer catalogue, live offer, automatic point valuation, approval or tax determination. Results are before unentered interest and other costs; all spending caps here are annual.

examples.title: Separate $630 of cash back from the fee and one-time bonus
examples.inputs: Annual eligible spending: $12,000 at 3% and $18,000 at 1.5%; no category caps; $95 annual fee; $200 one-time bonus; no usable credits.
steps: Add the rewards, then subtract the $95 fee for recurring net value. Include the $200 bonus only in the first-year illustration.
examples.answer: Gross annual cash back is $630; recurring net value is $535 and first-year value including the entered bonus is $735.

examples.title: Value 60,000 annual points at an entered one cent each
examples.inputs: $30,000 annual eligible spend at 2 points per dollar; no cap; 1 cent per point; $95 annual fee; 20,000-point one-time bonus; no credits.
steps: Multiply $30,000 by 2 to obtain the recurring points earned.
At the entered redemption assumption, points are worth $600 before the fee. The bonus adds $200 only once.
examples.answer: The plan earns 60,000 annual points: $505 recurring net value or $705 in the bonus year at the stated redemption value.

examples.title: Compare a 2% card with a $95 fee against a fee-free 1% card
examples.inputs: Same $30,000 annual eligible spending for both plans; Plan A earns 2% with a $95 fee; Plan B earns 1% with no fee; no credits.
steps: Plan A gives $600 − $95 = $505 recurring net rewards.
Plan B gives $300 recurring net rewards. Subtract B from A using the same spending amount.
The $95 fee is offset at $9,500 annual spending for these flat rates. Interest, late fees and promotional bonuses are not included.
examples.answer: Plan A has a $205 recurring annual advantage at the entered $30,000 spending level.

expected.label: Recurring annual net advantage (A minus B)

questions.question: Are points worth one dollar each?
questions.answer: No. The input is cents per point. At 1 cent each, 60,000 points have an assumed value of $600. Actual redemption terms can differ.

questions.question: Are category caps monthly or annual here?
questions.answer: Annual spend caps only. Monthly spending is annualized, but monthly and quarterly cap resets are not simulated.

questions.question: Does the calculator recommend a bank card?
questions.answer: No. It evaluates your manually entered reward rules and fees without a bank catalogue, live offer or approval check.

questions.question: Does the first-year bonus repeat in annual results?
questions.answer: No. The recurring result excludes the bonus. The first-year result adds only the one-time amount you assumed is earned.

sources.title: Chase: Guide to credit card rewards programs

accounts-receivable-turnover.summary: Receivables turnover compares period net credit sales with representative average trade receivables. Using the same definitions, average-balance DSO converts that turnover into collection days. Reporting-period days and the balance method are part of the result.
accounts-receivable-turnover.scope: Matched-period net credit sales and trade receivables only. The two-point average may miss seasonality. DSO uses average balances here; no closing-balance, countback, aging, bad-debt or customer-credit analysis is provided.

examples.title: Convert 12 annual receivables turns into about 30.42 collection days
examples.inputs: 365-day reporting period; $300,000 net credit sales; $25,000 representative average trade receivables.
steps: Divide net credit sales by average receivables: $300,000 / $25,000 = 12.
Divide 365 reporting days by turnover. Keep cash sales out of a credit-sales denominator.
examples.answer: Turnover is 12 times for the year and average-balance DSO is about 30.42 days. This does not identify the age of any particular invoice.

examples.title: Average $20,000 and $30,000 receivables balances before calculating
examples.inputs: 365-day year; $300,000 net credit sales; beginning receivables $20,000; ending receivables $30,000.
steps: The two-point average is ($20,000 + $30,000) / 2 = $25,000.
Use that average with same-period net credit sales. Seasonal sales or a large year-end balance change may need a better average.
examples.answer: The inputs reproduce 12 annual turns and about 30.42 collection days, rather than using only the ending balance.

questions.question: Can I use total revenue instead of net credit sales?
questions.answer: Only if it represents the credit sales corresponding to the selected receivables. Cash sales and unrelated revenue should not be silently included.

questions.question: Is the turnover result annualized?
questions.answer: No. It is turnover for the selected reporting period. The DSO calculation uses the day count you enter.

questions.question: Why is my published DSO different?
questions.answer: A company may use closing balances, another receivables population or a countback method. This tool uses a representative average and matching net credit sales.

questions.question: What happens when the denominator is zero?
questions.answer: Turnover and DSO are checked separately. Undefined results are labeled explicitly rather than displayed as infinity or a real zero multiple.

days-payable-outstanding.summary: Days payable outstanding converts a matched-period trade-payables balance into an estimated payment period. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy versions can give different answers. This worksheet names the denominator and reports payables turnover alongside the days measure.
days-payable-outstanding.scope: Manual trade payables and matched credit purchases or a named COGS proxy. No inferred credit-purchase share, full inventory roll-forward, supplier aging, contract-term approval or cash-solvency decision.

examples.title: Ten payables turns imply 36.5 payment days in a 365-day year
examples.inputs: $50,000 average trade payables; $500,000 same-period net credit purchases; 365 reporting days.
steps: Payables turnover is $500,000 / $50,000 = 10.
DPO is $50,000 / $500,000 × 365. Match the trade-payables balance to the purchases financed by those suppliers.
examples.answer: DPO is 36.5 days. Compare it with actual supplier terms and payment records before judging payment behavior.

examples.title: Use beginning and ending payables to estimate the same average
examples.inputs: Beginning trade payables $40,000; ending trade payables $60,000; annual net credit purchases $500,000; 365 days.
steps: Average the balances to obtain $50,000.
Divide average payables by matching credit purchases and multiply by 365. A two-point average can hide seasonal swings.
examples.answer: The estimated average produces 36.5 DPO, matching the known-average purchase-based case.

examples.title: A $400,000 COGS proxy changes the estimate to 45.625 days
examples.inputs: Same $50,000 average payables and 365-day year; substitute $400,000 cost of goods sold for credit purchases.
steps: The result differs from purchase-based DPO because the denominator changed. It does not show that the company actually paid suppliers later.
examples.answer: The COGS-proxy result is 45.625 days. Label the proxy when comparing it with a purchase-based result.

questions.question: Is COGS exactly the same as credit purchases?
questions.answer: No. Inventory changes, cash purchases and accounting adjustments can make them differ. The COGS mode is an explicit proxy.

questions.question: What goes into average accounts payable?
questions.answer: A representative trade-payables balance for the same purchase or cost period. Beginning/end mode uses the two-point arithmetic mean.

questions.question: Can I calculate a quarter’s DPO?
questions.answer: Yes. Enter that quarter’s purchases or selected cost, average trade payables and actual reporting days.

questions.question: Does a longer DPO mean bills should be delayed?
questions.answer: No. The ratio does not determine supplier terms or whether payments are overdue or appropriate.

cash-conversion-cycle.summary: The cash conversion cycle combines inventory days and collection days, then subtracts payables days. The operating cycle stops before that subtraction. Keeping all three components on compatible definitions allows a meaningful comparison between known-days and financial-input calculations.
cash-conversion-cycle.scope: Manual, matched-period balance ratios or supplied component days. Purchase-based and COGS-proxy payables are separate modes. This is not a cash-balance forecast, liquidity guarantee or supplier-payment instruction.

examples.title: A 75-day operating cycle becomes a 15-day cash conversion cycle
examples.inputs: Inventory days 45; collection days 30; payables days 60; all entered on compatible definitions.
steps: Add inventory and collection days: 45 + 30 = 75.
Subtract payables days: 75 − 60. The operating cycle and cash conversion cycle are different measures.
examples.answer: The cash conversion cycle is 15 days; the operating cycle is 75 days. Neither is a cash-balance forecast.

examples.title: Derive each component before combining financial-statement inputs
examples.inputs: 365 days; average inventory $80,000; COGS $400,000; average receivables $25,000; net credit sales $600,000; average payables $50,000; credit purchases $500,000.
steps: Combine the unrounded components: inventory days + collection days − payables days.
examples.answer: The purchase-based cash conversion cycle is about 51.71 days under these matching annual inputs.

examples.title: Changing only the payables denominator changes the reported cycle
examples.inputs: Use the same 365-day balances, COGS and credit sales as the preceding case; use COGS as the disclosed payables proxy.
steps: Inventory and collection days remain 73 and about 15.2083.
Subtract this different payables estimate. A lower cycle here is a definition change, not evidence of an operating improvement.
examples.answer: The COGS-proxy cycle is about 42.58 days. Keep the denominator convention consistent in comparisons.

questions.question: Can the cash conversion cycle be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. A negative result can indicate that modeled collections occur before supplier payments. It is retained and explained.

questions.question: Is operating cycle another name for CCC?
questions.answer: No. Operating cycle equals DIO plus DSO. CCC subtracts DPO as well.

questions.question: Why do two calculators give different CCC values?
questions.answer: They may use different balance averages, credit-sales scope, periods or purchase-versus-COGS payables denominators. Compare each component and input definition.

questions.question: Does CCC predict when the business will run out of cash?
questions.answer: No. That requires available cash and cash-flow assumptions. CCC summarizes working-capital timing ratios.

sources.title: OpenStax: Working capital and cash cycles

roic.summary: ROIC compares annual after-tax operating profit with representative average invested capital. It differs from accounting net-income ROE and a general profit-to-cost ROI. The numerator, capital definition, tax assumptions and reporting period must describe the same operating scope.
roic.scope: Annual manual operating-profit and invested-capital assumptions only. No live financial statements, balance-sheet reconstruction, intangible-capital adjustment or stock valuation. Loss tax benefits are not presumed unless explicitly selected.

examples.title: Compare 12% ROIC with an entered 8% WACC
examples.inputs: Annual NOPAT $150,000; representative average invested capital $1,250,000; entered WACC 8%.
steps: Divide annual after-tax operating profit by average invested capital and express the ratio as a percentage.
Subtract the entered WACC in percentage points. On the same capital base, simplified economic profit is $150,000 − 8% × $1,250,000.
examples.answer: ROIC is 12%, a 4-percentage-point spread over the assumed WACC; simplified annual economic profit is $50,000.

examples.title: Convert $200,000 EBIT to $150,000 NOPAT at a 25% tax assumption

values.loss_tax: No assumed tax benefit on a loss

examples.inputs: Annual EBIT $200,000; entered operating tax rate 25%; no assumed tax benefit on a loss; average invested capital $1,250,000; WACC 8%.
steps: For this positive EBIT case, simplified NOPAT = $200,000 × (1 − 25%) = $150,000.
Divide that operating numerator by average capital. Do not silently substitute net income after financing costs.
examples.answer: The simplified tax bridge gives 12% ROIC. An entered tax rate does not establish actual cash taxes or a tax deduction.

examples.title: Average $1 million and $1.5 million of invested capital
examples.inputs: Annual NOPAT $150,000; beginning invested capital $1,000,000; ending invested capital $1,500,000; WACC 8%.
steps: The two-point capital average is $1,250,000.
Use the same annual NOPAT and WACC assumptions as the known-average example. More frequent balances may better represent material within-year changes.
examples.answer: ROIC is 12% using the estimated average. The matching denominator makes it comparable with the first case.

questions.question: Can I use net income instead of NOPAT?
questions.answer: Not silently. NOPAT is operating profit after tax; net income can include financing and non-operating items. Match the earnings and capital scope.

questions.question: Does a loss automatically create a tax benefit here?
questions.answer: No. The default EBIT mode assumes no tax benefit on an operating loss. Applying the simplified tax rate requires an explicit selection.

questions.question: What is the difference between a percent return and a percentage-point spread?
questions.answer: ROIC 12% minus WACC 8% is a 4-percentage-point spread. It is not a 4% relative increase in return.

questions.question: Is invested capital always the market value of debt and equity?
questions.answer: No. Operating/book definitions and adjustments vary. The tool asks for a consistently defined average and does not reconstruct it from market prices.

sources.title: Morgan Stanley: Return on invested capital

interest-coverage-ratio.summary: Interest coverage divides EBIT by borrowing interest expense from the same reporting period. For example, $100,000 EBIT and $25,000 interest give 4 times coverage. The result describes an earnings-to-interest relationship; it does not show whether cash can cover principal repayments or every other obligation.
interest-coverage-ratio.scope: Manual matched-period EBIT and borrowing-interest expenses, or a simple signed net-income/tax bridge. No EBITDA model, cash-flow forecast, lender approval, default probability or universal covenant threshold.

examples.title: $100,000 EBIT covers $25,000 annual interest four times
examples.inputs: Same 12-month period: EBIT $100,000; borrowing interest expense $25,000; selected coverage target 3 times.
steps: Divide $100,000 by $25,000. EBIT is earnings before interest and income taxes; use an amount covering the same business and reporting period as interest.
At the selected target, required EBIT is 3 × $25,000 = $75,000. Compare that with actual EBIT to find $25,000 headroom.
Principal repayments, capital expenditure and working-capital cash needs are outside this interest-only denominator.
examples.answer: Coverage is 4 times. The entered 3-times target is a comparison assumption, not a lending approval or a universal safety threshold.

examples.title: Rebuild $100,000 EBIT from net income, tax and interest
examples.inputs: Same reporting period: net income $56,000; income tax expense $14,000; interest expense $30,000; target 3 times.
steps: Add the signed income-tax amount and interest back to net income: $56,000 + $14,000 + $30,000 = $100,000.
Divide by the same $30,000 interest expense. The target requires $90,000 EBIT, leaving $10,000 headroom.
Use this simple bridge only when those three statement amounts reconcile to the EBIT definition you need; a covenant may require other adjustments.
examples.answer: Coverage is about 3.3333 times. Both numerator and denominator matter: this differs from the first case despite matching EBIT.

examples.title: An operating loss produces negative interest coverage
examples.inputs: Same 12-month period: EBIT −$10,000; interest expense $25,000; selected target 3 times.
steps: Divide −$10,000 by $25,000. Preserve the negative sign rather than interpreting the result as zero debt or spare earnings.
At the entered 3-times target, required EBIT is $75,000. Relative to the −$10,000 actual amount, the modeled EBIT shortfall is $85,000.
examples.answer: Interest coverage is −0.4 times. This is an earnings deficit, not a default prediction or a cash-flow forecast.

questions.question: Is interest coverage the same as DSCR?
questions.answer: No. This ratio uses EBIT and interest expense only. DSCR has its own income definition and debt-service denominator, typically including principal.

questions.question: What if interest expense is zero?
questions.answer: The ratio has no defined denominator. The tool labels it explicitly and does not print infinity or a real zero multiple.

questions.question: Can the coverage ratio be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. Negative EBIT divided by positive interest produces a negative multiple.

questions.question: Is the target multiple a recommended safe minimum?
questions.answer: No. It is a user-selected scenario. The tool does not read covenants, select a lending threshold or predict default.
